claim: Streptococcus pyogenes causes mild human infections as well as life-threatening invasive diseases.
source: Streptococcus pyogenes causes mild human infections as well as life-threatening invasive diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about S. pyogenes pathogenicity that is established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations known to enhance virulence account for only half of the severe invasive infections.
source: Since the mutations known to enhance virulence to date account for only half of the severe invasive infections, additional mechanisms/mutations need to be identified.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous research and provides rationale for the current study.

claim: The study conducted a genome-wide association study of emm89 S. pyogenes strains to identify pathology-related bacterial genetic factors.
source: Here, we conducted a genome-wide association study of emm89 S. pyogenes strains to comprehensively identify pathology-related bacterial genetic factors (single-nucleotide polymorphisms [SNPs], indels, genes, or k-mers).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The Japanese cohort study included 311 emm89 strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The global cohort study included 666 emm89 strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 17 SNPs/indels were associated with invasiveness in the Japanese cohort.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section with supporting data.

claim: 1075 SNPs/indels were associated with invasiveness in the global cohort.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section with supporting data.

claim: 2 genes were associated with invasiveness in the Japanese cohort.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section with supporting data.

claim: 169 genes were associated with invasiveness in the global cohort.
source: Japanese (n = 311) and global (n = 666) cohort studies of strains isolated from invasive or non-invasive infections revealed 17 and 1075 SNPs/indels and 2 and 169 genes, respectively, that displayed associations with invasiveness.
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and detailed in the results section with supporting data.

claim: The fhuB T218C mutation is a non-invasiveness-related point mutation.
source: We validated one of them, a non-invasiveness-related point mutation, fhuB T218C, by structure predictions and introducing it into a severe invasive strain and confirmed that the mutant showed slower growth in human blood.
evidence: This is validated through experimental data showing the mutant's slower growth in human blood.

claim: The fhuB T218C mutant showed slower growth in human blood compared to the wild-type strain.
source: We validated one of them, a non-invasiveness-related point mutation, fhuB T218C, by structure predictions and introducing it into a severe invasive strain and confirmed that the mutant showed slower growth in human blood.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from bactericidal assays presented in Figure 7.

claim: In 2005, more than 0.6 million people were estimated to have invasive S. pyogenes infections.
source: In 2005, more than 0.6 million people were estimated to have invasive S. pyogenes infections (Carapetis et al., 2005), and the reported incidence of invasive S. pyogenes infections continues to increase globally (Craik and Hla, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carapetis et al., 2005.

claim: The reported incidence of invasive S. pyogenes infections continues to increase globally.
source: In 2005, more than 0.6 million people were estimated to have invasive S. pyogenes infections (Carapetis et al., 2005), and the reported incidence of invasive S. pyogenes infections continues to increase globally (Craik and Hla, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Craik and Hla, 2022.

claim: The mortality rate of patients with STSS remains high, ranging from 23% to 81%, even with proper treatment.
source: However, even with proper treatment, the mortality rate of patients with STSS remains high, ranging from 23% to 81% (Walker et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2014.

claim: No safe and effective commercial vaccine against S. pyogenes has yet been licensed for human use.
source: Moreover, although several protective vaccine candidates against S. pyogenes exist, no safe and effective commercial vaccine has yet been licensed for human use (Brouwer et al., 2023; Yamaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brouwer et al., 2023 and Yamaguchi et al., 2013.

claim: S. pyogenes has been classified into at least 240 emm types based on a hypervariable region sequence of the emm gene.
source: S. pyogenes has been classified into at least 240 emm types based on a hypervariable region sequence of the emm gene, which encodes the M protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of S. pyogenes classification.

claim: The hypervariable region of the M protein is responsible for type-specific antigenicity.
source: This hypervariable region of the M protein is responsible for type-specific antigenicity and binds with high affinity to C4b-binding protein, a major fluid phase inhibitor of the classical and lectin pathways of the complement system that confers resistance to opsonophagocytosis (Bessen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessen et al., 2018.

claim: The hypervariable region of the M protein binds with high affinity to C4b-binding protein.
source: This hypervariable region of the M protein is responsible for type-specific antigenicity and binds with high affinity to C4b-binding protein, a major fluid phase inhibitor of the classical and lectin pathways of the complement system that confers resistance to opsonophagocytosis (Bessen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessen et al., 2018.

claim: Since the mid to late 2000s, emm89 strains have been increasingly isolated from samples obtained from patients with invasive diseases.
source: Since the mid to late 2000s, emm89 strains have been increasingly isolated from samples obtained from patients with invasive diseases, becoming one of the most frequently identified lineages in developed countries (Ikebe et al., 2021; Fay et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ikebe et al., 2021 and Fay et al., 2021.

claim: In the United Kingdom, no more than 10 cases of invasive diseases caused by emm89 S. pyogenes were reported annually in the 1990s.
source: For example, in the United Kingdom, no more than 10 cases of invasive diseases caused by emm89 S. pyogenes were reported annually in the 1990s.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2015.

claim: In the United Kingdom in the 2010s, approximately 150 cases of invasive diseases caused by emm89 S. pyogenes were reported out of the 1000–1500 invasive cases caused by all emm types of S. pyogenes in each year.
source: In the 2010s, however, approximately 150 cases were reported out of the 1000–1500 invasive cases caused by all emm types of S. pyogenes in each year (Turner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Turner et al., 2015.

claim: In Japan in 2018, emm89 strains were isolated from 36% of patients diagnosed with S. pyogenes-induced severe invasive infections.
source: In 2018, emm89 strains were isolated from 36% of patients diagnosed with S. pyogenes-induced severe invasive infections, following emm1 strains, which were isolated from 57% of patients (Ikebe et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ikebe et al., 2021.

claim: S. pyogenes emm89 strains have been genetically sub-clustered into three clades according to the nga promoter region patterns and the presence/absence of the hasABC locus.
source: S. pyogenes emm89 strains have been genetically sub-clustered into three clades according to the nga promoter region patterns and the presence/absence of the hasABC locus, which is responsible for hyaluronan capsule synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2015 and Zhu et al., 2015a; Zhu et al., 2015b.

claim: Clade 3 is distinct from clades 1 and 2 in terms of overexpression of virulence factors NADase and SLO, owing to mutations in the promoter region of the nga-ifs-slo operon.
source: Clade 3 is distinct from clades 1 and 2 in terms of two features: overexpression of virulence factors NAD glycohydrolase (NADase) and streptolysin O (SLO), owing to mutations in the promoter region of the nga-ifs-slo operon, and the lack of a hyaluronan capsule (Turner et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015a; Zhu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2015 and Zhu et al., 2015a; Zhu et al., 2015b.

claim: Clade 3 lacks a hyaluronan capsule.
source: Clade 3 is distinct from clades 1 and 2 in terms of two features: overexpression of virulence factors NAD glycohydrolase (NADase) and streptolysin O (SLO), owing to mutations in the promoter region of the nga-ifs-slo operon, and the lack of a hyaluronan capsule (Turner et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015a; Zhu et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2015 and Zhu et al., 2015a; Zhu et al., 2015b.

claim: There was no difference in the isolation frequencies of clade 3 strains between invasive and non-invasive diseases in Japan.
source: We previously reported no difference in the isolation frequencies of clade 3 strains between invasive and non-invasive diseases, at least in Japan, and concluded that the mutations in clade 3 are not responsible for the gain of invasiveness (Hirose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirose et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations in the two-component system CovR/S promote high virulence during infections caused by emm1 S. pyogenes.
source: During infections caused by emm1 S. pyogenes, mutations in the two-component system, CovR/S, promote high virulence (Walker et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2007.

claim: CovR/S mutations cause the upregulation of DNase, hyaluronan capsule, IL-8 protease, C5a peptidase, streptokinase, NADase, SLO, and superantigen SpeA.
source: These mutations cause the upregulation of DNase, hyaluronan capsule, IL-8 protease, C5a peptidase, streptokinase, NADase, SLO, and superantigen SpeA, as well as the downregulation of cysteine protease SpeB and streptolysin S (SLS) (Walker et al., 2007; Sumby et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2007 and Sumby et al., 2006.

claim: CovR/S mutations cause the downregulation of cysteine protease SpeB and streptolysin S (SLS).
source: These mutations cause the upregulation of DNase, hyaluronan capsule, IL-8 protease, C5a peptidase, streptokinase, NADase, SLO, and superantigen SpeA, as well as the downregulation of cysteine protease SpeB and streptolysin S (SLS) (Walker et al., 2007; Sumby et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2007 and Sumby et al., 2006.

claim: Nonsense mutations in covR and/or covS are present in 46.3% of S. pyogenes strains isolated from severe invasive infections in Japan.
source: Epidemiologically, Ikebe et al. reported that nonsense mutations in covR and/or covS are present in 46.3% of S. pyogenes strains isolated from severe invasive infections in Japan, but only 1.69% of isolates from non-severe ones (Ikebe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ikebe et al., 2010.

claim: Nonsense mutations in covR and/or covS are present in only 1.69% of S. pyogenes isolates from non-severe infections in Japan.
source: Epidemiologically, Ikebe et al. reported that nonsense mutations in covR and/or covS are present in 46.3% of S. pyogenes strains isolated from severe invasive infections in Japan, but only 1.69% of isolates from non-severe ones (Ikebe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ikebe et al., 2010.

claim: The covR/S mutation is not responsible for all invasive clinical strains.
source: Moreover, these studies indicated that the covR/S mutation is not responsible for all invasive clinical strains.
evidence: This is inferred from the epidemiological data showing that only 46.3% of severe invasive strains have covR/S mutations.

claim: A total of 207 clinical isolates were collected with the cooperation of the National Institute of Infectious Diseases and 10 public health institutes nationwide.
source: A total of 207 clinical isolates were collected with the cooperation of the National Institute of Infectious Diseases and 10 public health institutes nationwide (Supplementary file 1, tables S2 and S3).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section.

claim: 150 of the 207 collected clinical isolates were determined as emm89.
source: In total, 150 of these were determined as emm89, followed by 24 and 19 strains as emm4 and emm12, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Japanese cohort consisted of 311 emm89 strains, including 135 severe invasive and 176 non-invasive isolates.
source: We combined these two sets and finally considered a total of 311 emm89 strains, including 135 severe invasive and 176 non-invasive isolates, as the Japanese cohort.
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section.

claim: In the Japanese cohort, 1417 core genes common to more than 99% of all isolates were determined out of the 3334 different genes detected within the 311 strains.
source: In the Japanese cohort, 1417 core genes common to more than 99% of all isolates were determined out of the 3334 different genes detected within the 311 strains.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The global cohort had 4743 different genes, of which 1327 were core genes.
source: In contrast, the global cohort was more diverse, with 4743 different genes, of which 1327 were core genes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The phylogenetic tree for the global cohort branched into four clusters: A, B1, B2, and B3.
source: The tree for the global cohort branched into four clusters, with clusters A, B1, B2, and B3.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cluster B3 included 640 genetically similar strains isolated mainly from Europe, North America, and Japan.
source: Cluster B3 included 640 genetically similar strains isolated mainly from Europe, North America, and Japan, whereas cluster A comprised 19 strains isolated from Oceanian countries, Kenya, Lebanon, the US, and Japan (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cluster A comprised 19 strains isolated from Oceanian countries, Kenya, Lebanon, the US, and Japan.
source: Cluster B3 included 640 genetically similar strains isolated mainly from Europe, North America, and Japan, whereas cluster A comprised 19 strains isolated from Oceanian countries, Kenya, Lebanon, the US, and Japan (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Within cluster B3, 522 strains (80.9%) were ST101, and 96 strains (14.8%) were ST646.
source: Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) analysis revealed that in cluster B3, 522 strains (80.9%) were ST101, and 96 strains (14.8%) were ST646 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ST646 was a Japan-specific lineage.
source: Notably, ST646 was the second most dominant type and a Japan-specific lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: ST101 and ST646 only differed in the 295th nucleotide in the murI locus.
source: Moreover, they only differed in the 295th nucleotide in the murI locus, one of the seven loci that determine MLST, suggesting that both lineages have a genetically close relationship.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by MLST analysis.

claim: Eight novel MLSTs were determined (ST1450, 1451, 1452, 1454, 1455, 1456, 1461, and 1463).
source: Eight novel MLSTs were determined (ST1450, 1451, 1452, 1454, 1455, 1456, 1461, and 1463) and 15 novel MLST strains were detected in the Japanese cohort (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 24,627 SNPs/indels were extracted from core gene alignments in the Japanese cohort.
source: We extracted SNPs and single-nucleotide indels from core gene alignments and detected 24,627 and 47,060 SNPs/indels in the Japanese and global cohorts, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: 47,060 SNPs/indels were extracted from core gene alignments in the global cohort.
source: We extracted SNPs and single-nucleotide indels from core gene alignments and detected 24,627 and 47,060 SNPs/indels in the Japanese and global cohorts, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The pan-GWAS of the Japanese cohort detected 17 SNPs/indels in 13 core genes.
source: The pan-GWAS of the Japanese cohort detected 17 SNPs/indels in 13 core genes (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1, table S5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Of the 17 significant variants in the Japanese cohort, there were 7 single-nucleotide deletions (SNDs), 7 SNPs causing non-synonymous amino acid substitutions, and 3 SNPs causing synonymous substitutions.
source: Of the 17 significant variants, there were 7 single-nucleotide deletions (SNDs), 7 SNPs causing non-synonymous amino acid substitutions, and 3 SNPs causing synonymous substitutions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The covS gene contains four SNDs with the lowest p-values in the Japanese cohort pan-GWAS.
source: The covS gene (also known as csrS), encoding a sensor kinase of the two-component system CovR/S, contains four SNDs with the lowest p-values (p = 1.16 × 10–7 for the 39th, 40th, and 46th nucleotides, and p = 1.15 × 10–6 for the 125th nucleotide).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claim: Four deletions in covS were associated with severe invasive infections.
source: These four deletions were associated with severe invasive infections.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The pan-GWAS for the global cohort detected 1075 SNPs/indels significantly related to invasive infections among the 360 core genes.
source: We also performed a pan-GWAS for the global cohort and detected 1075 SNPs/indels significantly related to invasive infections among the 360 core genes (Figure 2B, C and Supplementary file 1, table S6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Among the significant SNPs/indels in the global cohort, 725 caused synonymous substitutions and 319 caused non-synonymous substitutions or frameshift mutations.
source: Among the significant SNPs/indels, 725 caused synonymous substitutions and 319 caused non-synonymous substitutions or frameshift mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: 19 SNPs induced nonsense mutations in the global cohort.
source: Moreover, 19 SNPs induced nonsense mutations, whereas the effects of 12 SNPs/indels were unpredictable because of a lack of reference sequences (Supplementary file 1, table S3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: 96 SNPs/indels accumulated in a single gene, murJ, which is involved in peptidoglycan biosynthesis.
source: Notably, 96 SNPs/indels accumulated in a single gene, murJ, which is involved in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, whereas 53 and 51 SNPs/indels were detected in murE and group_1008, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SNP with the lowest p-value (p = 1.35 × 10–14) in the global cohort was in lacE, which encodes the EIICB component of the lactose-specific phosphotransferase system.
source: The SNP with the lowest p-value (p = 1.35 × 10–14) was lacE, which encodes the EIICB component of the lactose-specific phosphotransferase system (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The lacE mutation was found to be associated with an invasive phenotype and mainly observed in strains isolated in the US.
source: This mutation was found to be associated with an invasive phenotype and mainly observed in strains isolated in the US.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: 10 SNPs/indels detected in the Japanese cohort were also detected in the global cohort, including 4 SNDs in covS and 1 SNP each in 6 loci.
source: Compared with the significant 17 SNPs/indels in the Japanese cohort, 10 SNPs/indels were also detected in the global cohort, including 4 SNDs in covS and 1 SNP each in 6 loci (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SNPs in six loci (gatA, group_1102, group_647, iscS_1, recU, and fhuB) were present exclusively in Japan.
source: In contrast, SNPs in six loci, gatA, group_1102, group_647, iscS_1, recU, and fhuB, were present exclusively in Japan (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1, table S6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Two significant genes were detected in the pan-GWAS for the Japanese cohort: group_184, which encodes a hypothetical protein, and divIC, which encodes a septum formation initiator protein.
source: Two significant genes were detected in the pan-GWAS for the Japanese cohort: group_184, which encodes a hypothetical protein, and divIC, which encodes a septum formation initiator protein (p = 8.81 × 10–6 and p = 6.72 × 10–6, respectively; Figure 3A and Supplementary file 1, table S7).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Analysis of the global cohort revealed the presence of 169 genes that were significantly related to invasiveness.
source: Although analysis of the global cohort revealed the presence of 169 genes that were significantly related to invasiveness, no genes were identical or homologous to the two genes detected in the Japanese cohort (Figure 3B, C and Supplementary file 1, table S8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Approximately 90% (152 of 169) of the significant COGs in the global cohort were found to be associated with non-invasiveness.
source: Approximately 90% (152 of 169) of the significant COGs were found to be associated with non-invasiveness.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Among the 169 genes in the global cohort, 37 encoded phage-related genes and 11 encoded mobile genetic elements (MGEs).
source: Among the 169 genes, 37 encoded phage-related genes and 11 encoded mobile genetic elements (MGEs) such as transposase, integrase, and recombinase.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The gene with the lowest p-value in the COG-based pan-GWAS for the global cohort was group_829, which encodes a transposase and is related to the invasive phenotype.
source: The gene with the lowest p-value was group_829, which encodes a transposase and is related to the invasive phenotype (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1, table S8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The k-mers-based GWAS detected two regions containing causative variants associated with severe invasiveness in the Japanese cohort.
source: In the Japanese cohort, the k-mers-based GWAS detected two regions containing causative variants associated with severe invasiveness (Supplementary file 1, table S9).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The complex comprising the nodes with the lowest q-value (q = 1.49 × 10–2) in the Japanese k-mers-based GWAS was Comp_11 in the covS locus.
source: The complex comprising the nodes with the lowest q-value (q = 1.49 × 10–2) was Comp_11 in the covS locus (Supplementary file 1, table S9).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The causative mutations in covS were an SND and 10 nucleotide polymorphisms.
source: The causative mutations in covS were an SND and 10 nucleotide polymorphisms (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The deletion in covS resulted in a frameshift mutation that shortened the length of CovS from 500 to 35 amino acids.
source: This deletion resulted in a frameshift mutation that shortened the length of CovS from 500 to 35 amino acids, leading to increased invasiveness, as previously reported in other emm types (Cole et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation to Cole et al., 2011.

claim: The k-mers-based GWAS for the global cohort identified mutations that were significantly associated with invasiveness in five regions.
source: Next, we analyzed the global cohort and identified mutations that were significantly associated with invasiveness in five regions (Supplementary file 1, table S10).
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The mutation with the lowest q-value (q = 1.90 × 10–2) in the global k-mers-based GWAS existed in Comp_7 and was identical to the SND in covS present in the k-mers-based GWAS of the Japanese cohort.
source: The mutation with the lowest q-value (q = 1.90 × 10–2) existed in Comp_7 and was identical to the SND in covS present in the k-mers-based GWAS of the Japanese cohort.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The invasive-related SNP in lacE substitutes the 554th glycine in LacE with valine.
source: The invasive-related SNP in lacE substitutes the 554th glycine in LacE with valine.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: LacE was predicted to be a membrane protein with nine transmembrane regions.
source: LacE was predicted to be a membrane protein with nine transmembrane regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold structural prediction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 554th residue of LacE is predicted to be in the intracellular EIIB domain.
source: As shown in magenta in the model, the 554th residue is predicted to be in the intracellular EIIB domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold structural prediction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: CovS forms homodimers.
source: Next, we predicted a homodimerized CovS model using AlphaFold, as the CovS of S. pyogenes forms homodimers (Jain et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jain et al., 2020.

claim: SOSUI predicted that CovS has two transmembrane regions.
source: SOSUI predicted that CovS has two transmembrane regions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on SOSUI prediction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations detected in the SNP/indel- and k-mers-based GWASes were predicted to shorten the CovS protein to 35 and 45 amino acids, respectively.
source: Mutations detected in the SNP/indel- and k-mers-based GWASes were predicted to shorten the CovS protein to 35 and 45 amino acids, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The SNP T218C in the fhuB locus substitutes the 73rd valine of FhuB with alanine.
source: As described above, the SNP T218C in the fhuB locus substitutes the 73rd valine of FhuB with alanine.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: FhuB is a component of an ATP-binding cassette transporter system that utilizes ferrichrome.
source: FhuB is a component of an ATP-binding cassette transporter system that utilizes ferrichrome, which is one of the carriers of Fe3+.
evidence: This is established knowledge about FhuB function.

claim: FhuB is predicted to localize to the cell membrane and form a channel with FhuG.
source: FhuB is predicted to localize to the cell membrane and form a channel with FhuG (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SOSUI suggested that FhuB and FhuG are 9-transmembrane proteins.
source: SOSUI suggested that FhuB and FhuG are 9-transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is based on SOSUI prediction.

claim: The 73rd residue of FhuB exists in a region adjacent to FhuD.
source: Therefore, we constructed a structural model of the FhuBCCDG complex (Figure 5D), which implied that the 73rd residue of FhuB exists in a region adjacent to FhuD.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold structural prediction shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The fhuB V73A mutation was predicted to induce formation of a small indentation on the molecular surface.
source: The mutation was predicted to induce formation of a small indentation on the molecular surface, thus increasing the surface area accessible to the solvent, and is considered to potentially affect the stability of the hydrophobic bond between FhuB and FhuD, and thus ferrichrome transport (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on structural prediction shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed that the differences in the overall transcriptional profiles between the WT and fhuB T218C strains were more remarkable in blood than in THY.
source: Principal component analysis revealed that the differences in the overall transcriptional profiles between the strains were more remarkable in blood than in THY (Figure 6A, B and Supplementary file 1, tables S11–S14).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The expression of CovR-regulating genes, including speB, nga-ifs-slo operon, and sag operon, was upregulated in the blood, compared to that in THY, in both the WT and fhuB T218C strains.
source: Among the overlapping genes, we found that the expression of CovR-regulating genes, including speB, nga-ifs-slo operon, and sag operon, was upregulated in the blood, compared to that in THY, in both the strains (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 1, tables S12 and S13).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In human blood, the fhuB T218C mutant strain resulted in the downregulation of mga and emm expression compared to the WT strain.
source: In human blood, the mutant strain resulted in the downregulation of mga and emm expression and upregulation of the expression of genes encoding virulence factors, such as speC, scpA/B, endoS, fba, ska, and sfbX, compared to those observed in the WT strain (Supplementary file 1, table S14).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: In human blood, the fhuB T218C mutant strain resulted in the upregulation of the expression of genes encoding virulence factors, such as speC, scpA/B, endoS, fba, ska, and sfbX, compared to the WT strain.
source: In human blood, the mutant strain resulted in the downregulation of mga and emm expression and upregulation of the expression of genes encoding virulence factors, such as speC, scpA/B, endoS, fba, ska, and sfbX, compared to those observed in the WT strain (Supplementary file 1, table S14).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: fhuB, fhuC, and fhuD were upregulated in the fhuB T218C mutant in both human blood and THY.
source: Notably, fhuB, fhuC, and fhuD were upregulated in the fhuB mutant in both human blood and THY (Supplementary file 1, tables S11 and S14).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: There were no differences in intracellular free ferric ion concentration between the WT and fhuB T218C strains in either THY or blood.
source: To determine whether fhuB T218C mutation affects iron transport, we measured the intracellular free ferric ion concentration in each strain and observed no differences among the strains in either environment (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At 2 and 3 hr after incubation in human blood, the fhuB T218C mutant strain exhibited a significantly decreased survival rate than that of the WT strain.
source: At 2 and 3 hr after incubation, the fhuB T218C mutant strain exhibited a significantly decreased survival rate than that of the WT strain (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on bactericidal assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: After incubation with erythrocytes, polymorphonuclear cells, or plasma, the fhuB T218C mutant strain exhibited a significantly lower survival index than that of the WT strain, at 2 and 3 hr after incubation.
source: Notably, after incubation with erythrocytes, polymorphonuclear cells, or plasma, the fhuB T218C mutant strain exhibited a significantly lower survival index than that of the WT strain, at 2 and 3 hr after incubation, as observed in whole blood (Figure 7C–E, G).
evidence: This is based on bactericidal assay data shown in Figures 7C-E and 7G.

claim: There were no significant differences between the survival rates of the WT and fhuB T218C mutant strains in heat-inactivated plasma.
source: However, there were no significant differences between the survival rates of the WT and mutant strains in heat-inactivated plasma, suggesting that the mutant strain is susceptible to complement (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on bactericidal assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The fhuB T218C mutant strain is susceptible to complement.
source: However, there were no significant differences between the survival rates of the WT and mutant strains in heat-inactivated plasma, suggesting that the mutant strain is susceptible to complement (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in survival between plasma and heat-inactivated plasma.

claim: The polymorphism T218C in fhuB impaired the survival of severe invasive strains in human blood through interactions with erythrocytes, polymorphonuclear cells, and complement.
source: Taken together, the polymorphism T218C in fhuB impaired the survival of severe invasive strains in human blood through interactions with erythrocytes, polymorphonuclear cells, and complement.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from bactericidal assays.

claim: By focusing on bacteria within closed phylogenies, false positives caused by confounding lineage effects were minimized.
source: By focusing on bacteria within closed phylogenies, false positives caused by confounding lineage effects were minimized, thus contributing to a higher level of accuracy of the pan-GWAS.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the study design.

claim: Spontaneous mutations in covR/S genes potentiate the transition from localized to invasive infection by M1T1 S. pyogenes.
source: Spontaneous mutations in covR/S genes potentiate the transition from localized to invasive infection by M1T1 S. pyogenes (Cole et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cole et al., 2011.

claim: Some SNDs in the covS locus were significantly related to the phenotypes in both the SNP/indel- and k-mers-based GWASes.
source: We demonstrated that some SNDs in the covS locus were significantly related to the phenotypes in both the SNP/indel- and k-mers-based GWASes.
evidence: This is based on the GWAS results presented in the study.

claim: Systemic invasive infections are caused by the overexpression of virulence factors through the inactivation of CovS, as a result of the introduction of a depletive mutation in the covS locus after infection.
source: Sumby et al. suggested that systemic invasive infections are caused by the overexpression of virulence factors through the inactivation of CovS, as a result of the introduction of a depletive mutation in the covS locus after infection (Walker et al., 2007; Sumby et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2007 and Sumby et al., 2006.

claim: emm89 clade 3 carries the identical promoter region pattern of the nga operon as emm1 strains.
source: In addition, emm89 clade 3 carries the identical promoter region pattern of the nga operon as emm1 strains, and the pattern conferred similarly high expression of nga and slo (Turner et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015a; Turner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turner et al., 2015, Zhu et al., 2015a, and Turner et al., 2019.

claim: A severe invasive Japanese strain without covS mutations increased the expression of speB, nga, slo, and genes in the sag operon in the blood.
source: Our RNA-seq data demonstrated that a severe invasive Japanese strain without covS mutations increased the expression of speB, nga, slo, and genes in the sag operon in the blood.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data from the study.

claim: covR/S mutations downregulate the expression of SpeB and SLS.
source: Although covR/S mutations downregulate the expression of SpeB and SLS, SpeB and SLS act as virulence factors, allowing S. pyogenes to invade host tissues (Terao et al., 2008; Sumitomo et al., 2011; Honda-Ogawa et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Terao et al., 2008, Sumitomo et al., 2011, Honda-Ogawa et al., 2013, and Lin et al., 2009.

claim: SpeB and SLS act as virulence factors, allowing S. pyogenes to invade host tissues.
source: Although covR/S mutations downregulate the expression of SpeB and SLS, SpeB and SLS act as virulence factors, allowing S. pyogenes to invade host tissues (Terao et al., 2008; Sumitomo et al., 2011; Honda-Ogawa et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Terao et al., 2008, Sumitomo et al., 2011, Honda-Ogawa et al., 2013, and Lin et al., 2009.

claim: Severe invasive infections have multiple gene expression profiles in addition to covR/S mutation-induced profiles within a single lineage, emm89.
source: These data suggest that severe invasive infections have multiple gene expression profiles in addition to covR/S mutation-induced profiles within a single lineage, emm89, and that the synergy between optimizing bacterial survival in human blood and upregulating multiple virulence factors contributes to the development of severe invasive infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and experimental data.

claim: The synergy between optimizing bacterial survival in human blood and upregulating multiple virulence factors contributes to the development of severe invasive infections.
source: These data suggest that severe invasive infections have multiple gene expression profiles in addition to covR/S mutation-induced profiles within a single lineage, emm89, and that the synergy between optimizing bacterial survival in human blood and upregulating multiple virulence factors contributes to the development of severe invasive infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq and experimental data.

claim: The FhuB mutation could increase bacterial susceptibility to free radicals generated in the presence of ferric ions in the blood.
source: First, the mutation in FhuB could increase bacterial susceptibility to free radicals generated in the presence of ferric ions in the blood.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed in the discussion.

claim: The Fenton and Haber–Weiss reactions generate hydroxyl radicals in erythrocytes.
source: Catalyzed by ferric ions, the Fenton and Haber–Weiss reactions generate hydroxyl radicals in erythrocytes (Cimen, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cimen, 2008.

claim: Iron in erythrocytes partially inhibits pneumococcal growth via a free radical-based mechanism.
source: Previously, we provided evidence that the iron in erythrocytes partially inhibits pneumococcal growth via a free radical-based mechanism (Yamaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2013.

claim: The FhuB mutation could affect bacterial transcriptional profiles and result in reduced fitness for survival in human blood.
source: Second, the FhuB mutation could affect bacterial transcriptional profiles and result in reduced fitness for survival in human blood.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed in the discussion.

claim: Lower emm transcription in the fhuB T218C mutant may lead to attenuated immune evasion.
source: Lower emm transcription in the mutant may lead to attenuated immune evasion.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing downregulation of emm.

claim: The M protein can bind C4-binding protein and factor H and inactivate the deposited C4b and C3b, leading to limited surface opsonization.
source: The M protein can bind C4-binding protein and factor H and inactivate the deposited C4b and C3b, leading to limited surface opsonization (Laabei and Ermert, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Laabei and Ermert, 2019.

claim: Antibodies against the ferrichrome-binding protein FtsB (FhuD) decrease blood bacterial burden and skin abscess formation in murine models infected with emm1 S. pyogenes.
source: Recently, He et al. reported that antibodies against the ferrichrome-binding protein FtsB, also known as FhuD, decrease blood bacterial burden and skin abscess formation in murine models infected with emm1 S. pyogenes (He et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2022.

claim: FhuD has been studied as a potential vaccine candidate against Staphylococcus aureus.
source: FhuD is a lipoprotein that has been studied as a potential vaccine candidate against Staphylococcus aureus (Nguyen and Götz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nguyen and Götz, 2016.

claim: The FhuBCCDG complex may be a promising target for vaccines against S. pyogenes.
source: Hence, this complex may be a promising target for vaccines against S. pyogenes.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings and previous research.

claim: The gene-based pan-GWAS revealed no significant correlation with the distribution of genes encoding virulence factors.
source: Our gene-based pan-GWAS revealed no significant correlation with the distribution of genes encoding virulence factors.
evidence: This is based on the GWAS results presented in the study.

claim: Changes in gene expression profiles cause invasive infections.
source: This finding minimizes the possibility that invasive infections are the result of the acquisition of virulence factors by non-invasive strains and indirectly supports the hypothesis that changes in gene expression profiles cause invasive infections.
evidence: This is inferred from the GWAS results.

claim: In the global cohort, 169 genes were related to the phenotype, including 37 phage- and 11 MGE-related genes.
source: In the global cohort, 169 genes were related to the phenotype, including 37 phage- and 11 MGE-related genes.
evidence: This is based on the GWAS results presented in the study.

claim: The genome of S. pyogenes is rich in prophages, phage-like chromosomal islands, and MGEs.
source: The genome of S. pyogenes is rich in prophages, phage-like chromosomal islands, and MGEs (Bessen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bessen et al., 2015.

claim: Prophages and MGEs sometimes function as vectors of virulence factors and antibiotic-resistance genes through interspecies and intraspecific transmission.
source: Prophages and MGEs sometimes function as vectors of virulence factors and antibiotic-resistance genes through interspecies and intraspecific transmission.
evidence: This is established knowledge in microbiology.

claim: Common superantigen-coding genes, such as speA, speC, speG, speH, speI, speJ, speK, and speL, and DNase-coding genes, such as spd1, are exogenous genes derived from prophages.
source: Common superantigen-coding genes, such as speA, speC, speG, speH, speI, speJ, speK, and speL, and DNase-coding genes, such as spd1, are exogenous genes derived from prophages (McShan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McShan et al., 2019.

claim: In the genome of S. pyogenes, there are broad MGEs where erm and mefA related to macrolide resistance and tetM involved in resistance to tetracyclines are located.
source: In addition, in the genome of S. pyogenes, there are broad MGEs where erm and mefA related to macrolide resistance and tetM involved in resistance to tetracyclines are located (Berbel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berbel et al., 2021.

source: On the other hand, a cluster comprising 49 non-invasiveness-associated genes including antibiotic-resistance genes was identified.
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis of COGs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: MLST analysis revealed that 522 of the 666 strains in the global cohort belonged to ST101.
source: In the present study, MLST analysis revealed that 522 of the 666 strains belonged to ST101.
evidence: This is based on MLST analysis presented in the study.

claim: ST646 was the second most prevalent lineage in the Japanese cohort and was not detected in any other country.
source: Following ST101, ST646 was the second most prevalent lineage in the Japanese cohort and was not detected in any other country.
evidence: This is based on MLST analysis presented in the study.

source: In addition, the difference between ST101 and ST646 was found only at the 295th nucleotide in murI, among the seven genes subjected to MLST typing.
evidence: This is based on MLST analysis presented in the study.

claim: All ST646 strains were isolated from the 4249 emm89 S. pyogenes strains in the MLST database PubMLST.
source: Furthermore, all ST646 strains were isolated from the 4249 emm89 S. pyogenes strains in the MLST database PubMLST (Jolley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on database analysis and supported by citation to Jolley et al., 2018.

claim: ST646 appears to be specific to emm89 strains and a unique lineage in Japan.
source: Therefore, ST646 appears to be specific to emm89 strains and a unique lineage in Japan.
evidence: This is inferred from the MLST analysis and database search.

source: Notably, Ubukata et al. also reported that ST646 strains began increasing after 2012, whereas the ST101 lineage was dominant until 2008 (Ubukata et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ubukata et al., 2020.

claim: ST646 is possibly a relatively new and Japan-specific lineage of emm89 S. pyogenes.
source: Taken together, we conclude that ST646 is possibly a relatively new and Japan-specific lineage of emm89 S. pyogenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MLST analysis and previous research.
